articles.title: GTA 6: four surprising ways playing video games could benefit your health
articles.author: George Farmer, PhD Candidate, Video Gaming and Psychological Wellbeing, Westminster University
articles.summary: From sharpening spatial skills to relieving stress, research suggests that playing video games can offer some unexpected health benefits.
articles.contentHtml:
After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, with fans around the world celebrating the latest instalment of one of gaming’s most successful franchises.

The excitement surrounding its release has also brought renewed attention to a familiar debate: what effect does playing video games have on us?

Gaming has long been associated with concerns about addiction and social isolation. But depending on what we play and how we engage with it, gaming can offer benefits for our cognitive abilities, social lives and physical and mental wellbeing.

1. Developing cognitive skills

Playing an action game such as Grand Theft Auto can be mentally demanding. Navigating a busy virtual city while driving, monitoring your surroundings and responding to unexpected events requires considerable attention and an ability to process information quickly.

A 2022 study of 163 adults compared regular action video game players, whose preferred games included Grand Theft Auto and Assassin’s Creed, with people who rarely or never played video games.

The gamers performed better on tests of mental rotation, the ability to imagine how an object would look if turned in a different direction. They were also more accurate at keeping track of multiple moving objects.

However, the researchers could not establish whether gaming had developed these abilities or whether people with stronger spatial and attentional skills were naturally drawn to action games.

A review of experimental studies found that playing action games could improve our ability to focus on relevant information while ignoring distractions, as well as our understanding of spatial relationships. These skills are useful in everyday activities such as navigating unfamiliar places.

However, researchers continue to debate how far the skills developed through gaming translate into broader improvements in our thinking and learning.

2. Building social connections

Despite the perception that gaming is an isolating activity, many modern games are designed around interaction with other people. Online multiplayer games allow players to communicate, collaborate and maintain friendships across geographical distances.

A study of 2,213 gamers and 287 non-gamers in Germany found that social gamers were generally as well connected as non-gamers, and that spending more time playing socially increased the likelihood of forming friendships online. These connections became particularly valuable during the COVID pandemic, when people had fewer opportunities to meet in person.

Some games also encourage players to work together towards a shared goal. In massively multiplayer online games, where large numbers of people play in the same virtual world, team members may need to plan their approach and share information.

For instance, research into team communication in the game World of Tanks found that higher-ranked teams tended to communicate more before battles, although this does not establish that gaming improves teamwork outside the game.

Of course, online gaming communities can expose players to harassment or abusive behaviour. The social experience depends on the game, its community and the people involved.

3. Promoting wellbeing and relieving stress

Gaming can be something to look forward to after a long day at work, offering a chance to relax and put everyday responsibilities aside.

Completing a difficult level or overcoming an obstacle can also satisfy our psychological need for competence: the feeling that we are capable of achieving something. Even an unsuccessful attempt gives players an opportunity to adjust their approach and try again.

Games often described as “cosy” are particularly appealing to people who prefer a slower pace, achievable goals and a relaxed atmosphere. My personal favourite is the Animal Crossing series, in which players live alongside animal characters and take on tasks such as gardening and crafting.

In interviews with 27 families, researchers found that Animal Crossing: New Horizons helped some parents and children cope with pandemic-related stress. The National Videogame Museum’s Animal Crossing Diaries collects players’ experiences of the game during the pandemic.

Some games are designed specifically for health or education rather than entertainment alone. Known as “serious games”, they can be used as part of mental health interventions. A review of therapeutic games for young people found promising effects on anxiety and depression, although more rigorous research is needed.

4. Encouraging physical activity

Not all gaming involves sitting still. “Exergames” incorporate physical movement into play, through activities such as dancing or sports simulations.

These games can make exercise more appealing to people who find conventional workouts less engaging. Research on virtual-reality exercise suggests that adding game elements can increase enjoyment during high-intensity interval training.

My favourite example of a game that encourages physical activity is Pokémon Go. It encourages players to walk around their neighbourhoods to collect digital creatures and visit locations, using augmented reality to add virtual objects to a view of the real world.

A study using fitness trackers found that the most engaged Pokémon Go players increased their activity by an average of nearly 1,500 steps a day over a month. Whether that increase lasts in the longer term is less clear.

Finding the right balance

None of these benefits is guaranteed. Gaming can become harmful when it interferes with sleep, work, education or relationships.

The World Health Organization recognises gaming disorder as a condition involving impaired control over gaming and continued play despite significant negative consequences. Simply spending a lot of time playing does not amount to a diagnosis.

Read more: From novels to GTA 6: the long history of fears about addictive entertainment

Why people play also matters. A review of research linked playing primarily to escape distressing experiences with problematic gaming, although those studies could not establish cause and effect.

Meanwhile, a large Oxford study found little evidence that the amount of time spent playing, on its own, substantially affected wellbeing.

While it is too early to establish the specific cognitive benefits of playing Grand Theft Auto 6, research into similar games suggests that navigating its virtual world could have some benefits.

Rather than judging all video games as good or bad, it is more useful to consider what people get from the games they enjoy and how gaming fits into the rest of their lives.

articles.title: South Africa’s child support grant ends at 18: the mental health impact is severe – research
articles.author: Tsepang Khumalo, Postdoctoral Researcher, Global Health, Erasmus University Rotterdam
articles.summary: A more thoughtful approach to children exiting the child support grant needs to be designed.
articles.contentHtml:
South Africa’s child support grant provides financial support to more than 13 million children in low-income households. It has become an essential part of the country’s social safety net, helping families meet basic needs and invest in their children’s health and education.

The grant ends in the month of their 18th birthday, when they are no longer legally children.

However, for many young South Africans, turning 18 brings little immediate financial independence, especially when faced with a labour market with exceptionally high youth unemployment. More than half of young people 15-24 who are actively looking for work cannot find a job. When the grant support is withdrawn, young people may have no reliable way to replace it with earnings. They may still be at school, trying to secure a place at university or college, or preparing to enter a labour market in which opportunities are scarce.

Losing R580 (US$35) a month can be a financial shock for households already struggling to make ends meet.

Considerable research has examined the benefits of receiving cash transfers. A recent review of the literature found strong positive average effects on a range of indicators, including school enrolment, food security, mental health, and child height-for-age. But surprisingly little attention has been paid to what happens when this support is withdrawn.

Our team of development economists from Stellenbosch University set out to address this in a recently published paper, examining what happens to mental health when young people lose access to child support grants. Theory suggests that it should have an impact on mental health, especially if it occurs during an important and often stressful life transition.

We found that teenagers experienced a substantial deterioration in mental health when they aged out of the grant. Based on these findings, we argue that the design of social support must consider exits more carefully. If support ends abruptly and traumatically, some of its gains may be at risk.

The impact

Our study followed almost 8,000 adolescents and young adults using data from South Africa’s National Income Dynamics Study, covering 2010 to 2017. By comparing young people before and after the eligibility cutoff and examining changes over time, we could distinguish the effects of losing the grant from the broader challenges of growing older.

We compared young adults a few months (less than a year) before their 18th birthday to young adults a few months (less than a year) after their 18th birthday. This window is selected to minimise the statistical error in the model.

Depressive symptoms were measured using the Center for Epidemiologic Studies 10-item self-report Depression Scale. It is a measure designed to assess symptoms of depression, with scores indicating the severity of depressive symptoms. It includes being bothered by things that don’t usually bother you, trouble keeping your mind on things you were doing, feeling depressed, not feeling hopeful about the future, feeling fearful, and struggling to “get going”.

We found a substantial increase in depressive symptoms when young people aged out of the grant. The deterioration was particularly pronounced immediately around the age threshold.

One reason for the increase in depressive symptoms was that just after losing the grant, young people were more likely to be looking for work compared with young people who were only a few months younger and who were still receiving the grant. This points towards the fact that these young people were experiencing pressure to find work, possibly to compensate for the loss of the grant.

The effects appeared particularly pronounced among young people in poorer urban households and those with limited alternative income sources. As expected, losing support is especially difficult when households have few financial resources to fall back on.

One interesting finding was that young people were more likely to look for work after losing the grant. At first glance, this might seem positive. After all, finding employment is an important step towards financial independence. But the interpretation is less straightforward in a country where jobs are exceptionally difficult to find. Among young people aged 15-34 about one in 10 are classified as discouraged workers, meaning that they are no longer actively looking for work, despite not having a job, and not being enrolled for further training or a qualification.

Increased job searching may reflect financial pressure rather than improved opportunities. Young people may feel compelled to look for work before completing their education or acquiring the skills they need.

Our study cannot establish that increased job searching explains the deterioration in mental health, but the findings are consistent with the possibility that young people respond to the loss of financial support by trying to replace it, often in difficult circumstances.

Is support being withdrawn too early?

The child support grant is designed to protect children from poverty and improve their prospects during their formative years. Yet the grant is withdrawn at an age when many are still economically dependent and face substantial barriers to completing their education and entering employment.

Adolescence and early adulthood are particularly important periods for mental health, education and the development of skills. Difficulties experienced during this transition can have lasting consequences. Poor mental health can make it harder to study, search for work and sustain employment. This raises the possibility that withdrawing support too abruptly may undermine some of the investments made in children during their earlier years.

We are mindful that South Africa faces severe fiscal constraints, and any extension of the child support grant would need to be carefully costed and evaluated. One option would be to consider transitional support for particularly vulnerable young people who are still completing school or moving into further education, training or employment. Another would be to strengthen the links between social grants and programmes that help young people make these transitions.

There may also be scope for phasing out financial assistance more gradually, rather than withdrawing it abruptly at a fixed age.

articles.title: Alcohol addiction and eating disorders often go hand in hand – here’s why
articles.author: Anna Preece, PhD Candidate, Disordered Eating and Alcohol, Bournemouth University
articles.summary: People receiving treatment for alcohol use problems are twice as likely to experience an eating disorder.
articles.contentHtml:
When some people drink, they purposely skip meals in order to amplify the effects of the alcohol or to save calories for their drinks. The practice, sometimes referred to as “drunkorexia”, highlights the crossover that can exist between risky drinking behaviour and disordered eating.

Although this practice has been documented in students and “wine-mom culture”, very little research has actually investigated how common it is in people who are in alcohol treatment services. This is what my research sought to do.

My colleagues and I recently conducted a review which found that eating problems are common among people being treated for alcohol addiction. We also found that the two conditions often share the same underlying drivers.

We reviewed data from 44 studies published between 1988 and 2026. Most of the studies were conducted with women living in high-income countries, including the US, Canada and the UK.

All the studies involved people getting support for their drinking. Some studies also included people getting support for their eating behaviour, while others only asked participants to fill in questionnaires about their eating habits.

Most studies were observational. This meant that rather than testing a treatment, people within these services were observed and asked about their experiences. This means our findings only show a link – we cannot prove cause and effect.

We found that people who are receiving treatment for alcohol use problems have around twice the likelihood of experiencing an eating disorder compared with the general population.

For instance, one of the studies we included in our review found that over two-thirds of women who were receiving treatment for alcohol addiction identified as binge eaters, while between 6% and 39% had bulimia nervosa.

Using food to cope with difficult emotions, manage mood or as a substitute for alcohol was common among both men and women undergoing treatment. Traits such as impulsivity, low self-esteem and negative self-image were common among study participants as well.

Several of the papers also showed that difficulties with mental health, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) were linked with increased risk of struggling with both an eating disorder and alcohol addiction.

Our study also showed that people undergoing treatment for alcohol addiction who are struggling with eating problems may be at increased risk of leaving treatment early, against medical advice. This can make recovery harder, increase the severity of challenging eating behaviour and the risk of medical complications.

Overall, our review highlights the distinct link between both alcohol addiction and disordered eating, and the common underlying traits both may share.

Our findings also suggest that asking people undergoing treatment for alcohol addiction about their eating behaviour could support treatment and highlight any challenges a person may be experiencing sooner.

Why this link matters

Both eating disorders and alcohol addiction can affect how the body absorbs nutrients, which may lead to nutrient deficiencies.

Weight gain may also be a problem in alcohol recovery, especially if a person uses sugar or food in order to cope. People who struggle with both of these conditions may also be at greater risk of depression or anxiety.

Using food and drink to cope with stressors, low mood or feeling bad about yourself is common – but many people may not be aware of when this behaviour becomes unhealthy or out of control.

For those undergoing treatment for alcohol use disorder, it may be beneficial to share any questions or concerns you may have surrounding food or eating with your therapist or nurse – including any challenging emotions you may have about food or meals.

Understanding the way both alcohol use disorder and disordered eating are connected means we may be able to better help those undergoing treatment for either condition.

articles.title: In It, Pennywise the clown is a powerful metaphor for OCD
articles.author: Aisleen Sturrock, PhD Student in Creative Writing, Aberystwyth University
articles.summary: Monsters are often used to represent mental health struggles, in both literature and film.
articles.contentHtml:
Monsters are often used to represent mental health struggles, in both literature and film. These creatures often act as physical stand-ins for internal battles, giving shape to feelings that are usually invisible and hard to explain. By turning psychological distress into something audiences can see and react to, writers and filmmakers make those experiences easier to understand.

In the It franchise, the central monster is Pennywise the clown. In my research I seek to challenge the trivialisation of OCD by portraying the fear and complexity of living with the condition – and to deepen understanding of OCD themes through prose. While Stephen King’s original 1986 novel includes a complex mythology, I have found that the 2017 and 2019 film adaptations simplify Pennywise into a figure that works surprisingly well as a metaphor for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD).

OCD is a condition in which a person experiences intense intrusive thoughts, known as obsessions. In response, people with OCD perform repetitive behaviours or mental acts called compulsions, to reduce distress or prevent a feared outcome. OCD can manifest itself through a range of different themes, often focusing on what someone values or fears most. For example, a person might worry they are a bad person because they dwell on a moment when they were slightly rude, or fear that stepping on a crack could harm a family member.

Eddie Kaspbrak, one of the main protagonists of King’s novel, experiences these kinds of compulsions. He has an intense fear of germs and illness that leads to a strong need for cleanliness, which he believes will prevent him from getting severe diseases.

This article is part of Rethinking the Classics. The stories in this series offer insightful new ways to think about and interpret classic books and artworks. This is the canon – with a twist.

Eddie fits with one of the most recognisable sub-types of the condition: contamination. This is a form of OCD in which someone believes that something has become contaminated by germs, illness, or even moral impurity such as sin. In response, they may engage in compulsive behaviour like frequent hand-washing, excessive cleaning of surfaces, or avoiding places and people they perceive as contaminated.

OCD and Pennywise

Played by Bill Skarsgård in the films It (2017) and It Chapter Two (2019), Pennywise’s strength builds from his ability to get into people’s heads. He feeds off the fear that grows through obsessions and remuneration. Remuneration is a compulsion in which a person repeatedly engages with intrusive thoughts, analysing them in an attempt to understand or resolve them. However this often makes the OCD cycle worse.

In It, the more the victim dwells on the fear, the stronger Pennywise becomes. This is similar to the way that when someone with OCD gives into their compulsions, their symptoms worsen.

Pennywise changes shape to match each child’s deepest fear. As the children become more frightened, he grows larger and more threatening. This mirrors the OCD cycle, where fear and avoidance reinforce intrusive thoughts, making them feel increasingly real and impossible to ignore.

In It: Chapter Two, Mike (Isaiah Mustafa) – one of the original frightened children, now a grown man – suggests that Pennywise knows “what scares [children] the most” and uses it to “salt the meat”. In both the film and novel, Pennywise appeared to Eddie as a diseased leper, directly targeting his intense fear of illness and contamination.

In the novel, Eddie experiences intrusive thoughts in his mother’s voice, something he calls his “mind-mother”. Eddie remembers his mother telling him he is “not like other people” and has “a very weak system,” reinforcing the idea that he is always at risk. Even after her death, her fears about sickness continue to control his behaviour. These internal warnings eventually become absurd in their extremity – “Eddie, get out of the taxi! They give you cancer!” – highlighting the exaggerated, catastrophic thinking typical of contamination OCD.

If Eddie’s mother’s voice represents his intrusive thoughts, then his inhaler (or his “aspirator”) is his compulsion. Even though, as an adult, he knows his inhaler was only ever a placebo, he still uses it in moments of stress. The irrationality of his fear doesn’t make it feel any less real.

In the novel, Eddie’s inhaler is repeatedly linked to violent imagery. In one section of the book, it is described like a weapon. Eddie stuffs it into his mouth and, “like miming suicide”, pulls “the trigger”. This unsettling comparison highlights how compulsions, while meant to provide relief, are harmful.

Later in the novel, Eddie’s compulsion of using his inhaler, meant to provide mental relief, is personified as a cruel voice that threatens him: “this time I might just kill ya!” This suggests that compulsions can become as frightening as the intrusive thoughts they are meant to control. Even knowing this, Eddie instinctively reaches for the inhaler, trapped in the familiar cycle of fear and temporary relief.

Eddie fights Pennywise and OCD

During the novel’s climax, Eddie turns his inhaler into a weapon against Pennywise, aiming it at the creature’s eyes. As he does, he imagines his mother’s voice warning him: “Don’t go near that Thing, Eddie! Things like that give you cancer!” This moment is important because Eddie doesn’t obey the intrusive thought – he challenges it. By using the object of his compulsion as a tool of resistance, Eddie symbolically pushes back against both his mother’s control and his disorder.

The final confrontation in the film adaptation It: Chapter Two (2019) also reflects real therapeutic ideas. Unlike in the novel, Pennywise isn’t defeated through brute force, but through psychological resistance.

The “losers” (as the kids describe themselves) insult and mock him, calling him “just a clown”. As they do, Pennywise physically shrinks and loses power. This mirrors Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), a therapy which encourages patients to let obsessions occur without completing the compulsion. Once Pennywise is no longer feared, he collapses, much like OCD loses its hold when compulsions are resisted.

It works as a striking metaphor for OCD. Each character is attacked through their deepest fears, and the more those fears are fixated on, the stronger Pennywise becomes. By turning intrusive thoughts into literal monsters, It captures the intensity of OCD’s internal struggles and offers a deeper, more empathetic understanding of the disorder and its emotional weight.

articles.title: Beyond DMT: why the true power of Brazil’s sacred jurema plant is social, not just psychedelic
articles.author: Aníbal G. Arregui, Profesor de Antropología, Universitat de Barcelona
articles.summary: The cult surrounding this psychoative plant is welcoming and diverse.
articles.contentHtml:
Jurema-preta is the name of both a plant – Mimosa tenuiflora – and an indigenous spiritual tradition of northeastern Brazil. The plant is used to make a potentially hallucinogenic brew that is consumed in sacred rituals. The exact mixture of herbs and other elements contained in the brew is a secret known only by jurema mestre shamans and never revealed.

In 2024 I had the opportunity to visit, as an anthropologist, the city of Natal, in Brazil’s Rio Grande do Norte region, which is a hotspot of the jurema cult. While there, I learned that jurema’s power is as much social as it is chemical.

The sacred and molecular properties of the plant are currently fostering all manner of exciting (though challenging) connections between indigenous knowledge and neuroscience. But jurema’s power goes beyond the plant and its ceremonies, as the jurema cult provides a radically plural space that welcomes all kinds of non-normative identities.

Therapuetic psychedelics

In recent years, neuroscientists from the Brain Institute of the Universidade Federal do Rio Grando do Norte, in Natal, have conducted groundbreaking research into jurema’s healing potential. In particular, they have found that the plant contains N,N-dimethyltryptamine, popularly known as DMT.

DMT is a powerful molecule that, when released into the brain, generates intense visions and induces states of trance.

But jurema’s effects are not just the result of ingesting DMT. As with the better known ayahuasca, the traditional recipe of the ritual brew is what allows DMT molecules to reach the brain. In their traditional preparation, both jurema and ayahuasca brews contain specific chemical inhibitors of the enzymes that would otherwise degrade the molecule in the stomach.

To date, it is unclear how indigenous peoples found the combination of plants and cooking techniques that allow DMT to make it through the stomach and reach the brain.

In recent years, there have been significant advances in research into the healing potential of substances such as MDMA, psylocibin, LSD and DMT. This psychedelic renaissance – which unites the fields of neuroscience, psychiatry and psychopharmacology – is finding new molecular pathways to treat PSTD, anxiety, addiction, and depression. DMT, in particular, seems to excel in mitigating depression.

Scientists at the Brain Institute in Natal have shown that the DMT extracted from jurema and inhaled by vaporisation has a rapid and powerful antidepressant effect, which can last for weeks.

But the institute is not just researching the plant and its molecules. It is also documenting – and engaging with – the Indigenous traditions that have been using this plant for centuries.

Science in dialogue with indigenous knowledge

In an innovative, non-traditional approach to research, scientists and jurema mestres have started to hold regular meetings to exchange perspectives on the plant. The goal is to include local communities and jurema shamans in a debate on how to respectfully relate to the sacred plant, while also pursuing scientific research into DMT as a possible treatment for a range of mental health issues.

This dialogue is, however, far from easy. While scientists at the Brain Institute try to approach the jurema with care towards other forms of understanding the plant, some mestres reject any scientific uses of any kind.

Recently, researchers at the Brain Institute have even abandoned the idea of extracting DMT from the jurema, focusing instead on synthetic DMT. But some shamans worry that the practice could become more widespread, and that other labs would not treat the plant with proper care and respect. These unresolved tensions are thoroughly described in a series of articles and a book by Brazilian journalist Marcelo Leite.

In his book, Leite notes a key aspect of current jurema cults, something I could confirm from my own ethnographic experience in Natal: most of the brews used in current rituals are not prepared in a way that allows DMT to reach the brain.

So, if its psychedelic effects are not always present, where does the power of the jurema reside?

A broad, accepting culture

In Natal, jurema rituals bring together all kinds of people and sensibilities. Following the work of anthropologist Luiz Assunção, an expert in the history of this religion, I was able to verify the richness, diversity and symbolic exuberance of the cult, which many practitioners consider as a science.

The variety of symbols that make up a jurema ritual is unfathomable. Each combines theological and spiritual references that range from indigenous animism to Catholic Christianity, Afro-Brazilian candomblé, spiritism, and even elements of Islam.

During my ethnographic survey in Natal, I attended rituals where practitioners danced, sang, played drums, took oaths and were seemingly possessed by spirits.

One of the most striking things I noticed is that many of the practitioners belonged to the LGTBQ+ collective. Many of these identities are not accepted in other religious traditions that are far more present in the region, such as evangelism. A 2023 book on Natal’s ancestral religion and culture includes a chapter on a trans woman who became a mestre juremeira.

The jurema plant has many interconnected potentials. One is its capacity to expand consciousness and induce states of spiritual trance. Another is the healing potential of DMT, which can have a powerful effect on symptoms of depression. But its most significant power is not molecular, but relational.

Both the plant and the cult create dialogue and connection between unlikely bedfellows: between indigenous peoples and neuroscientists, and between people with traditional and non-normative identities. The power of the jurema therefore also lies in creating connections between radically different kinds of people.
